content:
discussion thread for the "Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search" paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763

Some quick observations:

  • I was hoping to see a direct comparison with informal AI solution methods - especially a number of problems where informal AI was convinced there is a solid solution, but attempting to formalized convinced everyone the attack method is futile, without having to resort to human experts. Instead the paper focuses on different variants of AI solvers with formalization and their comparisons. There is a mention of the informal AI solver - Aletheia (from https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10177) but no head-to-head comparison.
  • the basic method (LLM <> lean compiler 'ralph loop') is surprisingly competitive, but it needs to be run multiple times. A version of the bitter lesson?
  • catching two misformalizations - erdos problem formal statements on the site were subtly wrong. This is a common thread that splitting formalizing statements without some validation testing through attempting to prove them results in misformalized statements.
  • failure analysis shows that allowing for "just some sorries for known results" is a bad idea

Failure Analysis. We analyzed the highest-scoring sketches (measured by Elo) across a random sample of problems on which our agent failed. First, the agent frequently offloaded a problem’s core difficulty into a single sorry within a helper lemma that reiterated the target statement in a slightly different form. Explicitly prompting against this behavior failed to prevent it. Second, for several problems, the top sketches relied on lemmas marked with sorry that the agent claimed were established results in the mathematical literature. Upon manual inspection, these lemmas proved to be hallucinations. These failure modes underscore the value of end-to-end formal verification.

  • the cost amounts per solved problem are not extremely high in the hundreds of $ range.

We built AlphaProof Nexus with the belief that the future of mathematics lies in human-machine partnership, where interactive AI tools serve to expand a mathematician’s creative capacity. Our results support this vision. Our mathematician collaborators found that proof attempts by our agents enhanced their understanding of a problem, even when an agent could not prove the claim at hand. Because the sketches were formal, experts could focus on the unresolved subgoals rather than re-verifying the entire argument.

This is the most exciting prospective to me - an AI solution attempt with formalization can get to some % competition, hit a roadblock and interact with a human researcher, who now can trust the rest of the chain of reasoning through formalization and think more deeply about a specific subproblem that has a formal statement.

Good comments!

Rado Kirov said:

  • the cost amounts per solved problem are not extremely high in the hundreds of $ range.

The paper makes a careful statement, "We do not intend USD as a comparison of AI and human mathematical labor." I think it's important to emphasize this point, that the paper's "cost" is primarily a relative measure of various computations, not an absolute measure. You can be sure that many decision-makers are eager to fire humans with the excuse that AI is cheaper, and we definitely need to push back against anyone who tries to use the costs in this paper for that purpose.
